This old-fashioned romantic comedy is based on the kind of story I loved as a teenager, but now find rather shallow and naive. In the case of May-September attachments, all that is on the mind of the older party is usually loneliness, or an inability to face the reality of aging, or both. And the younger is most likely looking for the kind of attention she (or he) lacked as a child. The underlying agendas seem more pathetic than romantic to me now; there is also something rather predatory about them. Dick Powell looked a bit embarrassed--as well as rather tired--as the elder lover in this romantic comedy. He was just turned fifty, attempting the role of a thirty-eight-year-old man romancing a teenaged girl. Jean Simmons was a knockout--pretty and charming, and full of energy--as the misbehaving seventeen-year-old presented as a kind of "gift" to the morally upright but lonely screenwriter, as a subject for him to study. Her spirited performance might have given me a higher rating for this film than I deserves. Anne Baxter was cast as the dutiful, somewhat brittle fiancée, and handled her small part deftly. Some of the dialogue is quite amusing, too, so it's not a total dud. 510

This is a pretty silly documentary that is just basically a compilation of clips from horror, science fiction and suspense movies. There are unnecessary shots of an audience watching the movie and Donald Pleasance and Nancy Meyers are the audience members who turn to the camera and explain why we like horror movies. Not only that, but all the reasons are obvious ("movie fear helps us deal with real fear", "we're at the mercy of the filmmaker in a theatre") and pretty clichéd. And the clips are shown so quickly that the changes are kind of jarring. And, taken out of context, these bits are not very scary at all. And it's REAL short--I rented it at a video store for $3.00 and was outraged that I paid $3.00 for a 20-minute movie. That being said, this is a good topic, and Kerr and Pleasance seem to have good intentions. For those who have an interest in knowing more about terror, it's interesting and informative. But if you're a horror fan (like me), you'll probably be bored stiff. Good concept, bad execution (no pun intended). 2 out of 3.

Creakiness and atmosphere this film has, but so unfortunately does the print I just viewed. Raymond Massey provides a laid back Sherlock Holmes, almost comically so in early scenes in his bathrobe, which he trades in for a laborer's garb to investigate the creepy mansion of Dr. Rylott (Lyn Harding). What wasn't clear to me was why Rylott would have wanted his stepdaughters dead. If as in the case of Helen (Angela Baddeley), he didn't want her to run off to get married, he would have accomplished the same thing by having her dispatched. Other curiosities abound as well. After setting an early wedding date with Helen, the fiancée is no longer heard from for the rest of the picture. The presence of a band of gypsies at the time of Violet Stoner's death provides merely a diversion, and what could have been an interesting murder tool, a poisonous snake, is diluted by the fact that it was not a cobra, the musical renderings of the Indian man servant notwithstanding. The Sherlock Holmes and the Saint film has expired, so unfortunately, the film cannot be viewed. The film provides a lot of interesting detail, almost comically so in some scenes. In one point, Holmes is almost mistaken for a man in Indian garb while visiting the creepy mansion of Dr. Rylott (Lyn Harding). What was most interesting to me was that Rylott would have introduced his stepdaughters to Holmes, and in the case of Mary (Angela D'Ocy), he would have wanted her to run off to get married, which would have accomplished his original goal by having Holmes killed. Other curiosities abound as well. Holmes has an awkward dinner date with Mary, whose fiancée is no longer heard from for the remainder of the film. The appearance of a band of gypsies on the time of Rylott's death serves as a diversion to explain what could have been the actual murder weapon, a poisonous snake, as well as the fact that Holmes is not a black man, the artistic renderings of a black man servant notwithstanding. W.C. Stewart competently plays the role of Dr. Watson, and he takes some getting used to if Nigel Bruce is not your cup of tea. As Rylott, Lyn Harding is sufficiently menacing, a trait that would be put to good use as Holmes' nemesis Professor Moriarty in two later films - 1939's "The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes" and 1939's "Murder at the Baskervilles". With repeated changes of actors and an interesting production plot, it's surprising that the story line isn't more disrupted than it is. The plot integrity is well maintained, even if it stretches a bit to fill in the gaps. I suppose that would be my only issue with the film, as I found some of the graininess in the picture quality to be a bit distracting. the asp.

Put simply, this mini-series was terrible. Let me count the ways. 1. Absurd plotting. 2. Over-acting. 3. Scattershot approach to characters. 4. Annoying narration. 5. Inability to create viewer interest. This film can't even pass the "Soap Opera for Dummies" test. I'm sorry I have not read this award-winning novel, so I am judging it only as a film, but it really stinks. Imagine going to a party where they show you dozens of appetizers. You look at the wide variety and want to taste them, but suddenly they are withdrawn, and you wonder where they went. That's like this film, with way too many characters introduced and never drawn out. There are enough stories and characters in this film to create a 20 episode series, yet we are given less than four hours to digest it all. There are more facial expressions and reaction shots of Ed Harris than you'll find on 10,000 monkeys. The pace is extraordinarily slow. Dennis Farina and Helen Hunt are so far over-the-top that their characters are not believable. Joanne Woodward's character is one-dimensional. The persistent river metaphor becomes trite. And, probably the most absurd part of the film--the cat. This evil and vengeful cat who follows the hero around to scratch him and his seat covers--well, come on now---it's not even good Stephen King! Probably the most interesting character in the film, and one who is not drawn well, is John Voss, the disturbed boy whose final act of desperation accounts for the only plot device that works in this film. Just about everyone in this film is unbelievable. To sum up, there's little here to inspire. The drama is poor melodrama. It's just a terrible effort.

Set on an abandoned spaceship 1000 years in the future and peopled with characters and crew right out of the 90's. The set is some industrial complex, like an oil tanker or whatever. Dave Lister is trying to get the best shot, standing in the corner. The dialog is filled with slang that's pretty dated ("yo, uh-oh, Daddy-O") but then maybe that's just the point. The most serious parts of the film are in the cargo hold, all in coffins a la Hotel Transylvania. The rest of the film is a full-on parody of the Alien and Alien franchise with gags, shameless rip-offs of all the best horror movies and song titles. At one point Casper VanDien even tells his crew to "kick the butt" in a dance scene. The film would have been better if they had just let everyone run with the satire but they keep attempting to make the film serious....maybe the backers were on the job that day. Anyway, the film is pretty killer if you're not too picky. FX are pretty good for the sets. END

Then, without warning, Jack decides to kill all the monsters. And then the movie ends. All in all, as a comedic homage to 1980s horror movies, Jack Brooks: Monster Slayer has plenty of potential but is purposeless and plods along like a snail's pace. Hopefully, these issues will be addressed before Jack 2: Desway to Hell or Jack vs. Freddy go into production
